name: McGill Big 3
lead: The McGill Big 3 is a trio of core exercises, the modified curl-up, the side bridge and the bird dog, associated with spine biomechanist Stuart McGill. People use it to build trunk endurance and a stable, upright midsection, which supports posture, a more neutral pelvis and the ability to keep training heavy without back flare-ups; in posture and looksmaxxing communities it is sometimes included in routines for anterior pelvic tilt [2][4]. McGill is a Canadian academic and Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo, a member of the Order of Canada since 2019 and the author of books including Low Back Disorders and Back Mechanic [1].

The exercises are described as training the abdominal, side and back muscles to stiffen the trunk evenly so the spine is stable without repeated bending; each position is typically held for about ten seconds, and endurance, not maximal strength, is the stated goal [4]. McGill's 2009 paper 'Exercises for Spine Stabilization: Motion/Motor Patterns, Stability Progressions, and Clinical Technique' presents the curl-up, bird dog and side bridge as its core exercises [5].

On T Nation, lifters mention the Big 3 as back rehab, a daily habit, a warm-up and a core day [6][7][8]. A 2020 case report implemented the routine in a person with an acquired brain injury to study its feasibility for balance and mobility [3]. No published study has tested the Big 3 for pelvic tilt or physique appearance.

paras: Stuart McGill's published books on back disorders and fitness include Low Back Disorders: Evidence Based Prevention and Rehabilitation, Ultimate Back Fitness and Performance, Back Mechanic and Gift of Injury. [1] The Big 3 are popularly associated with his spine biomechanics work, but the encyclopedia entry does not describe the exercises.

Stuart McGill's ideas are summarised in the ACE Fitness article as: trunk muscles stiffening in a balanced way create spine-sparing stability, and fatigue leads to poor movement patterns that are more likely to cause back pain, so endurance matters more than strength [4]. The article says removing the source of tissue strain matters as much as exercise [4].

The curl-up is a small lift of the head, shoulders and chest as one unit while lying on the back with one knee bent and hands under the lower back to preserve its natural arch [4]. The side bridge is a hold on the forearm, with knees bent or legs straight for more challenge, lifting the hips into a straight line [4]. The bird dog is an opposite arm and leg raised parallel to the floor from hands and knees with hips level [4].

The bird dog is named in Wikipedia's core stability article as a back-muscle exercise, and the plank as an abdominal exercise. [3] The same article says research support for the core stability model is limited and cites a critical review titled "The myth of core stability". [3]
Wikipedia's pelvic tilt article suggests planks, side planks and dead bugs for anterior pelvic tilt, which overlap in purpose with the Big 3 though not the same movements. [2]

Forum posts show how the routine is used: one lifter calls for 'the McGill Big 3 every day' for a back that hurt after deadlifts [7], another includes it in warm-ups [8], and another scales it to be more challenging for a core day [9]. A poster asks how to program the bird dog and plank because articles conflict [10].

The 2020 case report in Neurology India describes implementing the Big 3 in an individual with acquired brain injury who walks independently, to evaluate feasibility for balance and mobility [3]. McGill's 2009 paper describes the exercises and their progressions [5]. No study found tests the Big 3 for pelvic tilt or appearance.

lore.intro: Lifters on T Nation treat the Big 3 as a go-to for back rehab and core work.

claims.claim: Doing the Big 3 daily keeps a lifter's back healthy.
claims.believers: Posters recommend daily Big 3 and McGill's rehab protocols for back problems [7][6].
claims.experts: The routine is attributed to McGill's biomechanics work and described as endurance for spinal stability [4][5]; the ACE article cites no specific trials.

claims.claim: Core routines like the Big 3 help correct anterior pelvic tilt.
claims.believers: Posture communities fold core exercises into pelvic-tilt routines [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia's pelvic tilt article suggests planks, side planks and dead bugs; its core-stability article notes research support for the core stability model is limited [2][11].

card.summary: A three-exercise back-sparing core routine tied to biomechanist Stuart McGill; thinly documented here and untested for looks.
card.note: Little source material; no appearance outcomes studied.

quick.overview:
The Big 3 are a curl-up, side bridge and bird dog associated with spine researcher Stuart McGill, used for trunk endurance with low spinal load.

Posture communities fold it into pelvic tilt and back routines. No study found tests it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: The exercises are described as training abdominal and back muscles to stabilise the spine without bending it repeatedly.
quick.risks: Low risk in general; back pain is usually referred to a clinician.

chain: Curl-up, side bridge and bird dog build trunk endurance
More stable trunk and neutral pelvis; fewer back interruptions to training
angle.text: People use the three holds as a daily core routine to keep the trunk braced and the pelvis neutral, aiming for better posture and a back that tolerates heavy training.
